title: HTTP fetching library for Node.js code: node-fetch, then native fetch
question: Which HTTP fetching approach should Node.js-side Backstage code standardise on: the third-party node-fetch package or the platform's built-in fetch?
context: ADR013 standardised backend code on node-fetch to avoid carrying several HTTP packages. The project later raised its minimum Node.js to 20, which ships a stable built-in fetch, and third-party fetch packages had shown problems on newer Node versions.

options.label: Several HTTP packages in use (axios, got and others)
Standardise Node.js code on node-fetch (ADR013)
Standardise Node.js code on native fetch, typed as typeof fetch (ADR014)

criteria: fewer dependencies and lower support burden

subQuestions: frontend code keeps using the framework fetch API reference (unchanged)
isomorphic packages take an injectable fetch (unchanged)
notableMoves: reversal was triggered by a platform change (raised minimum Node.js), not by dissent
the superseding ADR repeats the unchanged frontend and isomorphic guidance and changes only the Node.js clause
old ADR kept in full with a banner pointing forward to its replacement

outcome.decision: All code executed in Node.js (backend and CLIs) uses the built-in fetch; node-fetch and similar replacement packages are phased out gradually.
outcome.rationale: Node.js 20+ has a stable undici-based fetch, and third-party packages were causing issues on newer Node versions.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: A single standard is picked among a few named libraries, per code context.
gaps: superseded or moved to another thread: Supersession as a first-class link: old record stays readable, marked no longer in force, with a forward pointer, and the new record cites the old. The design has Reopen (same question returns to open) but no Supersede that creates a new settled question pointing back at the old.

provisional decision: Reversal trigger is an environmental change (minimum platform version raised), not a new argument. The record has 'What we knew at the time' but nothing like 'revisit when X changes' or a recorded watch condition.

consequences and obligations: Consequences carry a follow-on obligation (msw 1.x based tests may break and need rewriting). The record's 'Built into' tracks PRs, not obligations created by the decision.

convention scope: One decision with three scopes (Node.js code, frontend, isomorphic packages), only one of which changed. The choice table holds a single answer, not per-context answers where one cell is revised.

evalUse: Clean supersession pair with an external trigger and a consequences section that anticipates test breakage; no debate recorded.
notes: Shallow clone has no history, so decision dates and authors are unknown (null). Neither ADR names people or an approver, so participants.count is null. Counted because ADR014 sets native fetch against the previously adopted node-fetch and ADR013 sets one standard against multiple packages. The underlying discussion (issue linked in ADR014 context, not read) is not captured; the debate itself is not recorded.

title: One shared Kubernetes cluster versus several clusters for service-team apps
question: Should service teams' dev, staging and production apps all run on one Kubernetes cluster, or should the platform split them across several clusters, and along what line?
context: In 2019 the team chose one cluster for everything, citing lower overhead and avoiding drift between environments. By 2021 it saw scaling limits, a single point of failure, risky upgrades and large blast radius, and proposed multi-cluster without deciding. In 2022, after moving to EKS and namespace growth from 409 to 457, it adopted a live/non-live split; in 2026 it went further to clusters per business unit.

options.label: Single cluster with namespaces separating dev/staging/prod (ADR012)
Multi-cluster, possibly with separate VPCs or AWS accounts per cluster (ADR021 proposal, decision left TBD)
Two clusters split by environment type: production and non-production (ADR036)
A live and a non-live cluster per business unit (ADR048, 2026)

subQuestions: how to move apps between clusters (kubecfg tokens, IP allow-lists)
AWS account per cluster (a later ADR)
whether users choose their own environment cluster
notableMoves: ADR012 was annotated in place twice (June 2020, May 2021) while still marked Accepted
ADR021 has a long argument but its decision section says only that it is to be decided; it was later marked superseded without ever being settled
ADR036 adopts multi-cluster but starts with only the live/non-live split and lets users self-select initially
ADR048 cites the noisy-neighbour and security gaps left by 036

outcome.decision: Adopt multi-cluster, starting with separate production and non-production clusters (ADR036), later extended to a live and non-live cluster for each business unit (ADR048).
outcome.rationale: Growth in namespaces and platform maturity made the single-cluster costs outweigh its benefits; separate clusters reduce blast radius, single points of failure and upgrade risk, at higher cost and complexity.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Alternatives are architectures compared on stated criteria; the early record is closer to an explore.
gaps: dormant or ownerless question: A question left 'TBD' for about 16 months and then replaced rather than settled: ADR021 holds a full argument and an empty decision. The design has Open and Settled only. There is no 'superseded without ever being settled' or 'parked' state, and Reopen assumes a prior answer exists.

superseded or moved to another thread: One underlying question has four numbered records over about seven years (012, 021, 036, 048). Reopen revisits the same question; this needs a lineage view across separately-numbered records showing who replaced which answer and why.

superseded or moved to another thread: Annotations appended to a record that stays Accepted (the 2020 and 2021 updates in ADR012). There is no light 'note on a settled question' that does not reopen it.

staged acceptance: Staged decision: adopt multi-cluster in principle, implement only the first split, leave user self-selection to be automated later. Settle yields one sentence and no 'step 1 of n' structure.

provisional decision: Evidence is a dated snapshot ('at time of writing' namespace counts, comparison against Kubernetes large-cluster limits). 'What we knew' could hold it, but nothing flags it for refresh when the numbers change.
consensus mechanics: Authority is the team, recorded as 'we decided', with no named person; the record's 'Settled by' face has nobody to show.

evalUse: Four-record chain on one question with an undecided intermediate record and in-place annotations; good for lineage and reopening tests.
notes: ADR012 is dated 01/06/2019; dates elsewhere in this repo are day-first and the ADR text mentions June 2020 as a later update, so it is read as 1 June 2019 (ambiguity noted). durationDays counts ADR021 (2021-05-11) to ADR036 (2022-09-16). No authors or approvers are named. The Google doc linked from ADR021 and the incident write-ups it cites were not read. Options were weighed inside ADR012 and 021 as pros and cons, not as a table.

title: Dedicated ingress controller per namespace versus shared controller pool
question: How should the platform stop its single shared nginx ingress controller crash-looping as its config grows: one load balancer and controller per namespace, or a managed pool of shared controllers?
context: All ingresses fed one very large nginx config behind one load balancer, and several controller pods were crash-looping. ADR018 chose a dedicated controller per namespace. The migration was started, then abandoned when AWS hard limits on network load balancers blocked it; ADR019 proposed a shared design, and an update weeks later removed the dedicated controllers entirely after another AWS limit hit during an upgrade.

options.label: Keep one default controller for every ingress
Dedicated load balancer and controller per namespace (ADR018)
Shared pool: default controller without the web application firewall, a managed pool with it, a few dedicated controllers left in place (ADR019)
All ingresses on the default controller with firewall annotations removed (update note on ADR019)

criteria: web application firewall coverage for production services

subQuestions: how many firewall-enabled ingresses one controller can safely carry
whether teams may define ingresses outside the environments repository
notableMoves: a rollout of ADR018 was started and aborted when AWS network load balancer limits were hit
ADR019 stays Proposed in the index while it was acted on
a dated update appended to ADR019 reports that a second AWS limit led to removing all dedicated controllers

outcome.decision: Dedicated per-namespace controllers were dropped; a shared design was proposed and then simplified so ingresses end up on the default controller without firewall annotations.
outcome.rationale: AWS hard limits (load balancers per VPC and zone, then security group rules) made the dedicated model impossible to operate.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Two architectures with concrete trade-offs, the second chosen after the first failed in practice.
gaps: reversal after shipping: Rejection came from implementation evidence (a quota nobody had checked), not from debate. The design has Spike (F3) before Settle; here the feasibility check happened after commitment, and there is no state for 'tried, failed, withdrawn' that preserves what the attempt taught.

superseded or moved to another thread: The replacement record stays 'Proposed' although it was acted on, and its real current answer lives only in an appended update note six weeks later. A settled answer that drifts after settling needs an amendment event, not just Reopen.
reversal after shipping: Incident reports are the evidence for the reversal. 'What we knew' lacks first-class incident links, and a reversal driven by an outage has no 'caused by' field.

coupled decisions: Three sub-decisions bundled in the replacement (disable the firewall on default, run a firewall-enabled pool, leave some dedicated controllers): coupled questions settled together with one status.
consequences and obligations: Cost consequences stated up front (more load balancers, pods and nodes); the record page has no section for accepted costs separate from rationale.

evalUse: Fast reversal driven by platform limits, with a still-Proposed replacement that was later amended; tests status semantics.
notes: Dates in ADR018/019 are written day-first (02/09/2020 and 09/09/2020), read here as 2 and 9 September 2020; the update note uses ISO 2020-10-14. durationDays is 018 to 019. No people are named; counted because both ADRs state options weighed and consequences. The linked Kubernetes issue and the incident log were not read.

title: Platform deployment pipelines: Jenkins, then Concourse, then GitHub Actions
question: What should run the platform team's deployment pipelines: its self-hosted Jenkins, a self-hosted Concourse, or GitHub Actions as used by the platform it is moving onto?
context: In 2018 the team replaced a fragile self-hosted Jenkins (about a week a month spent reviving it, recurring outages, blocked product teams) with Concourse on Kubernetes. In 2026, with the platform moving into the Modernisation Platform's accounts and pipelines, it decided to switch to GitHub Actions and retire Concourse and its management cluster.

options.label: Keep self-hosted Jenkins
Self-hosted Concourse on Kubernetes (ADR003, 2018)
GitHub Actions, using the Modernisation Platform pipelines where possible (ADR040, 2026)

criteria: pipelines as code and cloud-native fit
alignment with the platform being joined

subQuestions: 2018: deploy Concourse on AWS or Kubernetes (settled by a spike ticket, listed under Consequences)
notableMoves: 2018 ADR lists tracker tickets as evidence and a struck-through success claim added later
the 2018 ADR is still marked Accepted although the 2026 ADR retires Concourse
the 2026 choice follows from a separate decision to move into another platform's accounts, so the tool choice is largely derived

outcome.decision: Switch deployment pipelines to GitHub Actions and decommission Concourse and its management cluster once the move is complete.
outcome.rationale: The platform is moving to the Modernisation Platform, which already uses GitHub Actions, so one pipeline system replaces the self-managed Concourse.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Tool selection among named alternatives, repeated eight years apart.
gaps: superseded or moved to another thread: The reversal is not recorded on the original: ADR003 is still shown Accepted and ADR040 gives the Concourse background in its own context. The design assumes the reopened question and its record are the same object; here the contradiction is spread over two unlinked records.

external authority: The real decider is an upstream strategy (join another platform). 'Decided elsewhere; we adopt' is not an authority type the design represents, and the options were effectively given.

nested follow-ups: The 2018 record's Consequences is a running to-do list with sub-decisions ('deploy to Kubernetes') and ticket ids. Sub-decisions hide in consequences and evidence lives in an external tracker.
consequences and obligations: Decommissioning is a stated future obligation tied to another migration finishing. 'Built into' tracks PRs, not 'retire X once Y completes'.

evalUse: Eight-year tool reversal where the old record was never updated; tests detection of an implied supersession.
notes: ADR003 date is 28/03/2018 (day-first read). ADR040 and ADR042 are both dated 2026-01-02. The ADR text says ADR039 relates to the move, but the file named 039 in the folder is about a network firewall and is dated 2025-09-16, so the cross-reference looks mismatched; not resolved here. Tracker tickets (CPT-xxx) were not accessible. Another team (alphagov/govuk-infrastructure ADR 0018, 2025) chose Concourse over Kargo in the opposite direction; see that record.

title: Core programming languages for platform automation
question: Which languages should the platform team use for the scripts, GitHub Actions and Lambda functions it writes and maintains?
context: In 2020 the team picked bash, Node.js and Python based on popularity across the organisation and a skills poll. By 2022 it found those skills thinner than assumed, was already learning Go for its testing tool, and saw other teams switch to Go with good results.

options.label: bash, Node.js and Python, each member choosing per problem (ADR004)
bash and Go, with Go the default for new scripts, Lambdas and tests (ADR019)
Java or .NET for Lambda

criteria: fit with the chosen testing tooling

subQuestions: migrating existing scripts to Go over time (no plan)
notableMoves: the 2020 decision rested on a team skills poll that tied between Node.js and Python (three each)
the 2020 ADR itself says it can be revisited; the 2022 ADR does so without a stated trigger
reversal justified by another team's positive experience

outcome.decision: Use bash and Go as the core languages; new scripts, Lambdas and tests default to Go.
outcome.rationale: The team lacked deep Node.js and Python skills, was already learning Go for Terratest, and could learn from other MoJ teams on Go; Go also has good Lambda start times.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Pick a language set against criteria; the earlier record shows a poll feeding the choice.
gaps: formal vote: A poll feeding a decision, tied 3-3, followed by a rule to let each member pick. The design has Ask and Takes (Agrees/Objects/Unsure) but no poll tally, no quorum, and no 'decide not to decide' outcome.
provisional decision: Both ADRs say they can be revisited, but neither names a review date or trigger. The design has no 'revisit when' condition on a settled question.
convention scope: A default-rule decision ('Go by default for new work') with legacy migration 'over time': a policy with scope and exceptions, not one sentence. No place for migration debt.
superseded or moved to another thread: The 2020 rationale (team skills) turned out wrong; 'What we knew at the time' captures the belief but nothing later records that it was disproved.

evalUse: Team-level reversal with an explicit tied poll in the first record; good for 'team versus individual authority' cases.
notes: No individuals are named in either ADR. The poll counts (three for Node.js, three for Python) are given without saying how many people voted. Cold-start and energy claims are cited by link in ADR019; the linked articles were not read.

title: Identity and access management for the platform's AWS accounts
question: How should people get access to the platform's AWS accounts without the team running its own joiners, movers and leavers process: IAM federation through GitHub, or AWS SSO with automated provisioning from a corporate identity provider?
context: Many people across the department needed access. Five weeks apart, one ADR described federation with GitHub as the identity provider and was then marked Rejected; the next chose AWS SSO with SCIM provisioning. A 2026 ADR later adds the organisation's enterprise identity service because GitHub-only access had become unsuitable for non-developers.

options.label: IAM federated access with GitHub as identity provider (ADR002)
AWS SSO with SCIM provisioning from a corporate identity provider (ADR003)
GitHub as identity provider behind SSO via Auth0

subQuestions: whether GitHub can still be the identity provider behind SSO
notableMoves: ADR002's body reads like a decision but its status says Rejected; the reason for rejection appears only in ADR003
ADR003 lists advantages and disadvantages relative to the rejected option
a 2026 ADR says GitHub Teams had always been the access route, which the 2020 pair does not explain

outcome.decision: Use AWS SSO with SCIM automated provisioning, managed at the organisation level, instead of IAM federated access.
outcome.rationale: Central, organisation-wide identity management with reusable permission sets across accounts outweighed losing alignment with two sister platforms and the lack of a Terraform provider at the time.
outcome.dissent: Trade-off acknowledged in the ADR: not aligned with the sister platform teams at that time; no named objector.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Two options compared in a pros and cons list, one rejected and one accepted.
gaps: rejected options content: A rejected record whose body reads as a decision. The reason it was rejected sits only in the next record. 'What we considered' lives inside the winning record, so a rejected option's own consequences are lost.

consequences and obligations: Per-option consequences are recorded as differences against the rejected option, a comparison matrix. The choice table holds cells, not long-form per-option advantages and disadvantages.

external authority: Scope-of-authority criterion: a team choice that binds an organisation-level root account (SSO is run at the department's root). The design has no field for 'who else does this bind'.
consequences and obligations: Joiners/movers/leavers control is a security-assurance concern. There is no way to mark a criterion as a control and attach an owner or risk.
implicit decision: Practice later diverged from the decision (the 2026 ADR describes GitHub Teams as the long-standing route) without a reversal record; long-lived decisions drift silently.

evalUse: Consecutive ADRs flipping within five weeks, with a later third record changing the practice; tests option-carryover across records.
notes: No individuals named. Dates: 0002 2020-09-15, 0003 2020-10-21, 0041 2026-02-13. ADR041 is listed as an extra source because it contextualises later practice; its own decision (take Entra ID into service, with language and group-approval sub-decisions deferred) is a separate decision not recorded here.

title: Application log collection and storage on the Kubernetes platform
question: How should application logs be collected and stored on the new Kubernetes platform: sidecar or node-level agent, Fluentd or Fluent Bit, and which store and UI?
context: Logging had to be a default service for all containers, with logs annotated by cluster metadata and searchable in a browser UI. The team expected it might later push logs to an organisation-wide store but wanted something running sooner.

options.label: Logging sidecar in every pod
Node-level agent as a DaemonSet
Fluentd as the agent
Fluent Bit as the agent
Managed Elasticsearch with Kibana
Push to an organisation-wide central log store

criteria: logging as a default service for all containers

subQuestions: control plane, node and kubelet logging (promised to a future ADR)
how to authenticate users to Kibana
notableMoves: status later changed to Deprecated with the label 'no superseding ADR'
scope restricted to application logs only

outcome.decision: Run a Fluent Bit agent on each node and send logs to the managed Elasticsearch service with Kibana; later marked deprecated without a replacement record.
outcome.rationale: A node agent meets the default-for-all requirement; Fluent Bit is lighter and easy to swap with Fluentd; the managed service gives search UI quickly.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Layered choices among named tools with trade-offs.
gaps: moot question: Deprecated with no successor: the decision was withdrawn rather than replaced, and the repo does not say what is now true. Settled and Reopen exist, but there is no 'retired, no replacement' state and a reader cannot find the current answer.
nested follow-ups: A promised follow-up decision (control plane and node logs) does not appear among the later ADRs in the folder. Open child questions promised in prose are not tracked.
conditional decision: Explicitly interim: chosen for now pending a possible organisation-wide store, a decision conditional on a future service owned by someone else.

consequences and obligations: Must-do obligations in Consequences (restrict Kibana access, explore SSO options) without owner or question; the design cannot turn a consequence into a follow-up question.
nested follow-ups: Two reversibility levels in one record: the agent is easy to swap, the store is not. Confidence is one value per record.

evalUse: Stack-selection ADR later deprecated without replacement; useful for status and 'current answer unknown' handling.
notes: Shallow clone: the deprecation date and who deprecated it are unknown (null). Status text is Deprecated (no superseding ADR). The ADR is dated 2021-08-16. No people named; options are weighed in prose so counted. The claim that no later ADR covers control plane logs is based on the 24 ADR titles in the folder, not on a full repo search.

title: Replace the CI/CD mix with Concourse after a Kargo versus Concourse trial
question: Which tool should replace today's mix of Argo Workflows, ArgoCD and GitHub Actions for building and deploying, after a security health check and the decision to leave Terraform Cloud?
context: An IT health check in 2024 flagged flaws in the deployment process, incidents had occurred, and the team had ongoing trouble with Argo Workflows. Leaving Terraform Cloud also created a need for something to apply Terraform automatically. A team design day picked two tools to trial.

options.label: Keep GitHub Actions, ArgoCD and Argo Workflows
Kargo for multi-stage promotion
Concourse CI
Run Concourse on virtual machines in EC2

criteria: fit with a Kubernetes-only operating model

subQuestions: in what architecture to deploy Concourse (later ADR)
how to write pipelines (later ADR)
notableMoves: a team design day chose which two tools to trial
each tool was prototyped on mock staging and production clusters by replaying the existing flow
Kargo was dropped because the feature needed was left undocumented by its maintainers and a workaround defeated its validation
findings were played back to the team before the decision

gaps: staged acceptance: Staged decision: the tool is chosen and two named follow-up questions are deliberately left to future records. The design can make child questions but not 'settled with named open follow-ups linked to this answer'.
evidence beyond check: Two parallel spikes, each with a verdict and an abandoned workaround, feeding option rows. F3 has one spike per question; per-option evidence is not modelled.

consequences and obligations: Explicit statement of a temporary double-maintenance cost during a staged migration; consequences are over time, not static.

notes: ADR dated 2025-08-12. ADR0014 (replace Terraform Cloud with S3 state, dated 2025-06-10) is an extra source: it states Accepted while its text says the ADR will move to accepted after migration, and defers a runner choice to a spike; not recorded as its own decision. title: Where Concourse runs and how artifacts are built and promoted
question: Where should Concourse run and how should artifacts be built, stored and promoted so deployments are secure, reproducible and visible across environments?
context: After choosing Concourse, the team spent roughly June to October 2025 on documents, conversations and meetings, and finalised the structure in team design sessions on 15 October 2025. Drivers were the 2024 health-check findings, user research with application teams and the move off Terraform Cloud.

options.label: Concourse on EC2 instances
One Concourse on Kubernetes in a central management cluster
A Concourse inside each environment's cluster
Separate infrastructure and application Concourses per environment
One Concourse on one cluster holding all environments (raised during the design day; ADR gives no reason it was not taken)

subQuestions: whether to version rendered manifests in Git
which YAML-generation tool to use (later ADR)
notableMoves: decision made in a team design session after months of side documents
a fifth option was raised on the day and discussed briefly
a build-once-and-promote rule was derived from flaky Rails asset precompilation
manifest versioning decided as a secondary outcome of the same session

outcome.decision: A blend of two options: a Concourse in each environment that deploys only there, plus a central 'tools' Concourse that builds artifacts once and cannot reach other accounts; rendered manifests will be versioned in Git.

off-platform decision: Inputs are three external documents (principles, platform vision, deployment options) not in the repo. Evidence off-platform needs durable capture or the record will point at links that rot.
rejected options content: A late option with no recorded reason for non-adoption: an option whose fate has no rationale.

convention scope: Reusable acceptance criteria ('core principles of secure CI/CD') are meant to judge future changes; criteria that outlive a single question are not representable.
consequences and obligations: Compliance: driven by an external security assessment; consequence statement claims it addresses the most critical findings, but evidence lives outside the record.

evalUse: Group-session decision with five options, hybrid outcome and a long consequences section.
notes: ADR dated 2025-10-16, one day after the design session. The Google documents it cites were not read. The ADR says most debate happened June-October 2025 across several places; none of that is captured, so durationDays is null. Count of participants unknown (the ADR names none). The 'consensus' label is my reading of 'the team landed on'; the ADR does not use that word.

title: Protective DNS from the national cyber security agency versus DNS firewall at platform level

context: The government protective DNS service was suggested as a way to improve customers' security. The team investigated it under an issue and compared it with a cloud-native firewall.

options.label: Implement NCSC protective DNS
Implement AWS Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall

criteria: provenance from a trusted government partner
ability to apply at platform level

subQuestions: scoping the DNS firewall implementation
notableMoves: investigation tracked in a GitHub issue (not read)
outcome is a rejection plus a substitute to be scoped

title: Organisation-wide guardrails for S3 encryption, staged rollout
question: Which service control policies should enforce stronger S3 encryption across member accounts, and how should they be rolled out without disrupting existing workloads?

Deny object writes that request the basic algorithm, applied broadly at OU level
Require a specific customer-managed key in conditions
Block customer-provided-key encryption as complementary hardening

criteria: reliability of each control proven by tests

subQuestions: when to require KMS keys (after pilot)
whether to apply object-level denies broadly
notableMoves: policy tests showed some assumed action names were invalid
a previous broad attachment caused an incident, shaping a pilot-first rollout
the Proposed status was unchanged at clone time, about 174 days after the ADR's date

title: Deprecate and remove the built-in Docker runtime shim from kubelet
question: Should Kubernetes deprecate and remove the in-tree Docker container runtime shim from kubelet, leaving Docker support to an external adapter?
context: The Docker shim lives in kubelet and is tied to its lifecycle, creating maintenance burden for developers and administrators when runtime issues arise, and inconsistent integrations. The proposal lists pros and cons, sets removal criteria and a multi-release plan.

options.label: Keep the shim in-tree
Deprecate in 1.20, then release kubelet without it (target 1.24) with an external adapter maintained by interested parties
Ship builds without the shim by default while keeping code in the tree for a while

subQuestions: graduating the CRI API (separate KEP)
out-of-tree Docker adapter ownership
Windows support on other runtimes
notableMoves: Drawbacks and Alternatives sections say none while the Motivation weighs pros and cons
removal gated on written criteria across several releases
user-facing deprecation FAQ and kubelet warning shipped in 1.20 before removal

outcome.decision: Deprecate the shim in 1.20 and remove it from kubelet by 1.24 once the criteria are met; Docker users move to an external adapter.
outcome.rationale: Docker should be one runtime among many; removing the shim reduces kubelet maintenance and lets the community move faster on runtime features.
outcome.dissent: Cons recorded: deployment pain from an extra binary, many affected users, CRI still alpha. No named objector in the KEP.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: A removal with alternatives limited to 'keep'; the weighing sits in prose.
gaps: conditional decision: Multi-release plan with criteria-gated steps (remove only once CRI is GA, e2e tests ready, etc.). The design has no timeline or gate checklist nor tracking of whether gates are met.
approval roster: Authors, reviewers and approvers named separately with SIG roles; the decider is a pair of approvers, not one 'Settled by' face.
consequences and obligations: Communication steps (migration guide, FAQ, warning) are part of the decision itself; the record has no 'announce' stage.
rejected options content: The weighing lives under Motivation while Alternatives says none, so a tool must find the options in prose rather than a table.
consequences and obligations: Large, unmeasured user impact and a rollback marked unsupported: a hard-to-reverse decision, while the record's confidence is one 'easy to change' line.
staged acceptance: Change of status from proposal to implemented is only visible in a history list and YAML fields.

evalUse: Deprecation-and-removal KEP with explicit removal criteria; weighing in prose, not in the Alternatives section.
notes: Read in full from raw.githubusercontent.com (kubernetes/enhancements master), not a clone, because the repo is large; the text is complete, not a summary. participants.count 7 = 2 authors + 5 reviewers named in kep.yaml; approvers (2) overlap the reviewer list. The KEP lists Drawbacks 'None' and Alternatives 'None' although cons are listed in Motivation. Mailing-list discussion linked in the KEP was not read. Implementation History dates are ambiguous (02/03/2022); durationDays left null.

title: Replace PodSecurityPolicy with a built-in admission controller
question: What should replace PodSecurityPolicy so Kubernetes can still limit privilege escalation through permission to create pods, given PodSecurityPolicy was deprecated instead of promoted to general availability?
context: PodSecurityPolicy had an awkward authorisation model, failed closed with no dry-run, and had an unbounded inconsistent API. The authors still wanted a built-in default control and proposed a validating admission plugin enforcing the Pod Security Standards through namespace labels.

options.label: Promote PodSecurityPolicy to general availability
New built-in validating admission controller enforcing the Pod Security Standards via namespace labels
Leave replacement entirely to third-party policy engines

criteria: can be switched on safely for fresh or upgraded clusters (dry-run, audit)

subQuestions: Windows support
automated migration tooling
default baseline for unlabeled namespaces
notableMoves: initial proposal provisionally accepted from a design document before the KEP merged
scope deliberately narrowed to avoid suppressing third-party policy engines and to avoid exemption creep
Drawbacks section just points to Risks; Alternatives point to three external documents
released behind a feature gate in alpha, beta and stable stages

outcome.decision: Add the built-in Pod Security admission controller (namespace-label policies in enforce, audit and warn modes) to replace PodSecurityPolicy, with a published migration path.
outcome.rationale: Keeps an out-of-the-box defence against privilege escalation while fixing PSP's rollout and authorisation problems.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Replacement design chosen against named alternatives, with strong requirements.
gaps: superseded or moved to another thread: A replacement decision that follows an earlier settled one (deprecate rather than GA). The new record needs a 'replaces' link to something outside the plan, plus a migration path as part of the answer.
approval roster: Sign-off needs named representatives from several teams (Windows, node, instrumentation, auth). That is a role-based approval roster, not 'ask a teammate for a take'.
off-platform decision: Alternatives are in three off-repo design documents; they must be imported or the record has no 'what we considered'.

consequences and obligations: A criterion about ecosystem effects: risk that a built-in standard becomes a de facto compliance requirement and suppresses third-party tools. The design has no 'who else is affected' field.

staged acceptance: Staged acceptance: accepted in principle from a design doc, then alpha, beta and stable with a feature gate. Maturity stages and gate criteria are not part of Settled or Built into.
nested follow-ups: Disabling the plugin is easy but removing PSP is not; reversibility differs for two actions in one record.

evalUse: Security-policy replacement KEP with explicit requirements, risks and staged graduation.
notes: Read in full from raw.githubusercontent.com (kubernetes/enhancements master), not a clone; text complete. participants.count 11 = authors (2), reviewers (4) and approvers (5) named in kep.yaml. The three alternatives documents were not read. Option 'leave replacement to third parties' is inferred from the ecosystem-suppression discussion and the goal of a built-in control; the KEP does not list it as a formal option. Calendar dates: provisional acceptance 2021-03-16, alpha 2021-08-04, beta release 2021-11-03; stable date not in file.

Reject AI-generated contributions entirely
Take no new action; existing contribution rules and the foundation policy apply

criteria: consistency with the foundation board's policy

roles: guests incl. emeritus and CPC rep

whether disclosure can be enforced
a dependent pull request waiting on this policy
notableMoves: live discussion scheduled for a time friendly to US-timezone members, vote to follow

Main repo stays authoritative; push changes out to the separate repo
Keep it in core to avoid coordination during security releases

whether to bring beneficiaries into a call
notableMoves: first meeting skipped part of the item because two relevant people were absent

Wait until Apple actually removes support

title: Choosing CPython's post-BDFL governance model
question: Which governance model should the CPython project adopt now that Guido has retired as BDFL: one of seven candidate PEPs, or continued discussion?
context: Guido's retirement left the project needing to choose how it would choose a governance structure. A working group at a core sprint drafted a voting process, and seven governance PEPs in the 8010 series competed, with the goal of resolving it before Python 3.8 and certainly before PyCon US 2019.

options.label: PEP 8016: five-person steering council elected by the core team
PEP 8010: technical leader model
PEP 8011: three-person leadership trio
PEP 8012: community governance model
PEP 8013: external council model
PEP 8014: commons governance model
PEP 8015: organisation of the Python community
Further discussion (make no choice yet)

criteria: use of mature, previously tested governance practice
legitimacy and secrecy of the vote

roles: PSF infrastructure director supervising the vote

subQuestions: voting method: Condorcet versus approval voting
public versus private ballots
whether incomplete rankings count
who should abstain
how ties and cycles are handled
notableMoves: the voting method was itself decided first through discussion and an approval poll among core developers
a review window preceded a two-week vote, and candidate PEPs were frozen during voting
a 'further discussion' choice was ranked alongside real options so voters could say none was good enough
private ballots won a poll after objections to public ones, with anonymised ballots published afterward
inactive core developers who intended to stay inactive were asked to abstain, without enforcement

outcome.decision: PEP 8016, the steering council model, won the core developer vote announced on 2018-12-17, and the other six models were rejected by the same vote.
outcome.rationale: For the winning model: be boring, simple, comprehensive and flexible, borrowing mature practice from another open source project. Reasons voters ranked it first are not recorded because ballots were anonymous.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: A ranked pick among eight named alternatives.
gaps: ranked choice: A formal ranked vote among full competing documents (Condorcet over seven candidates plus a 'none yet' sentinel), run by an outside trusted party. The nearest primitive is a stance pill on a take, with no ranking, eligibility roll or quorum.

formal vote: Secret ballot was a stated requirement, chosen by an earlier poll. The design shows faces, names and reasons on Takes, so it cannot hold anonymous votes or publish anonymised ballots afterward.
nested follow-ups: A meta-decision (how to decide how to decide) with its own PEP, resolved before the object-level question. Nested questions with an ordering constraint are not modelled.
formal vote: Options are independent documents with their own authors and change histories, frozen while the vote runs. There is no option owner and no freeze or lock of options during a vote.
rejected options content: Losers are first-class records that point to the winner (status Rejected, see winner). 'What we considered' is only a list of names.
staged acceptance: Time-boxed phases (review window, then vote window, results on a fixed day) have no counterpart; the design has no deadline or phase for a question.

evalUse: Process decision with a formal ranked vote, eight options and a nested voting-method decision, all documented in repo text.
notes: PEP 8001 read in full, PEP 8016 read in part (acceptance note, rationale, specification headings and amendment rule), and PEP 8010's rejection note, from clone (python/peps clone at commit 6068058). The results announcement is linked from the PEPs on a discussion forum that could not be fetched, so vote counts and ballot detail are not recorded. Statuses of 8011 to 8015 were checked from their headers. durationDays runs from PEP 8001's creation date (2018-08-24) to the 2018-12-17 result. The seven PEP authors in options come from the candidate list inside PEP 8001. Original decider wording (v0): vote of the CPython core developers by ranked ballot (Condorcet method).

title: Assignment expressions (the walrus operator)
question: Should Python get an expression form of assignment, and if so with what syntax, precedence and scoping rules?
context: Naming a value is only possible in statements, so comprehensions and conditions cannot capture sub-results without refactoring. Similar proposals had come up repeatedly on the ideas list. The PEP lists many alternative spellings and scoping variants that were weighed and rejected.

options.label: NAME := expr as an operator that binds like ordinary assignment
expr as NAME
expr -> NAME
Statement-local names marked with a leading dot
A where: block attached to a statement
TARGET from expr
Capture only in if and while statements
Statement-scoped (sublocal) names to avoid namespace pollution
Lower precedence so most conditions need no parentheses
Allow an unparenthesised tuple on the right-hand side
Always require parentheses
Change comprehension scope rules as part of this PEP

criteria: no confusion with existing as syntax

subQuestions: precedence of the operator
scope of the target inside comprehensions and class bodies
evaluation order in dictionary comprehensions
when parentheses are required
notableMoves: the PEP header lists nine posting dates between February 2018 and August 2019
a scope-rule change for comprehensions was withdrawn so the PEP could stay focused
the sublocal-scope idea from earlier revisions was dropped for simplicity
the PEP argues for judging by real code, with appendix findings from reading standard-library code, rather than toy examples
after acceptance and before release the spec was amended: a dedicated exception subclass was dropped and use in comprehension iterables was restricted

outcome.decision: Accepted by the BDFL in July 2018 (the PEP header links the resolution message) and shipped in Python 3.8, with spec amendments made before release.
outcome.rationale: Naming sub-expressions inline helps comprehensions, conditions and debugging, and the chosen operator avoids the conflicts and awkwardness of the alternative spellings while keeping scope rules simple.
outcome.dissent: The PEP records recurring objections (why not make = an expression, why keep statements, namespace pollution) and answers them; remaining individual dissent is not recorded in it.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: A syntax and semantics choice among many named alternatives, plus coupled scope and precedence sub-choices.
gaps: delegated decider: The decider (BDFL) is also a co-author. The design has no conflict-of-interest marker, and the closest analogue is the asker pressing Settle, which conflates champion and decider.

off-platform decision: Decision recorded as a pointer to a mailing-list message after nine rounds of a living document. 'What we knew at the time' would need snapshots of each revision because the PEP is edited in place.

rejected options content: Rejected ideas are a dozen separate entries, each with its own mini-argument and code example. The source treats them as first-class content, while 'What we considered' lists option names only.

coupled decisions: Coupled sub-decisions (spelling, precedence, target scope, parentheses, comprehension scope, evaluation order) were accepted together. The model must either make each a question or fold them into one card.

evidence beyond check: Evidence was real-code reading (standard-library examples and an appendix essay) with a stated norm against toy examples. Research modes in the design do not include 'examples from real code'.
superseded or moved to another thread: The spec was amended between acceptance and release. F6 Reopen implies a full reopen, not a small patch recorded on the settled answer.

evalUse: Well-known language decision with a dozen explicit rejected alternatives and an author who is also the decider.
notes: PEP read in the relevant sections from clone (python/peps clone at commit 6068058): header, rationale, spec-changes, rejected alternatives, objections and appendix start. The resolution link is a mailing-list message that was not retrievable here, so the acceptance wording and exact date are not read. durationDays is null because the header gives no exact resolution date; participant and comment counts are not in the PEP. Proposers are null where the PEP does not attribute an alternative. Original decider wording (v0): BDFL (also a co-author).

title: Optional global interpreter lock in CPython
question: Should CPython accept a build mode that runs without the global interpreter lock, given single-thread overhead, an ABI split and the cost to the extension ecosystem?
context: The lock limits multi-core use, which matters for scientific and AI workloads. The author, an outside contributor with a core-developer sponsor, proposed a build flag with biased reference counting, per-object locks and a new allocator, and measured overhead on a standard benchmark suite.

options.label: Accept the PEP: a --disable-gil build mode, with a later path toward one build
Keep the lock and use multiprocessing for parallelism
Keep the lock and release it inside C extensions
Parallelise inside native libraries
Use a concurrent garbage collector
Merge the two builds into one runtime-switchable lock in later phases

criteria: multi-core use for scientific and AI workloads

subQuestions: a three-phase path to a single build mode through about 2030
specialisation under free threading
mitigating single-thread slowdown
handling of borrowed references in the C API
notableMoves: a second discussion thread was opened in May 2023, per the PEP's post history
the council's acceptance is a note on the PEP with conditions, announced on a discussion forum
the council reserved the right to roll back the whole change if it proves too disruptive

outcome.decision: Accepted by the steering council on 2023-10-24 on condition that rollout is gradual, breaks as little as possible, and can be rolled back, including reverting the entire PEP.
outcome.rationale: Not in the PEP text; only the conditions are noted. The acceptance announcement is on a discussion forum that could not be fetched.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Accept or decline against alternatives, with a measured cost to weigh.
gaps: conditional decision: Conditional, staged acceptance by a body: first phase accepted with provisos and a standing right to roll back everything. The design has Settled plus Reopen and no 'accepted with monitored conditions' state or condition tracker.

delegated decider: A council decides over the author, and neither the author nor the sponsor can settle. There is no flow where the asker hands the question to a decision body and the result comes back from another platform.

staged acceptance: A multi-year roadmap sits in the doc (three phases to around 2030) where only phase one is decided. Later phases are open issues to revisit on a schedule or condition, not on a person pressing Reopen.

conditional decision: The trade-off turns on benchmark numbers (about 5 to 8 percent overhead) and ecosystem readiness that keep moving after acceptance. 'Decision conditional on a measured threshold' has no home in the design.
votes as evidence: Key stakeholders are ecosystem classes (scientific and AI library maintainers, extension authors), represented as motivation sections. Takes models individual teammates.
rejected options content: Rejected ideas and open issues are explicit sections of the source, i.e. first-class content on the record.

evalUse: Council-decided, conditionally accepted proposal with a multi-phase roadmap and explicit performance numbers.
notes: PEP read in the relevant sections from clone (python/peps clone at commit 6068058): header and acceptance note, performance, alternatives, rejected ideas and open issues. The acceptance post and discussion threads linked from the header could not be fetched, so rationale, vote split and dissent are unknown. durationDays runs from creation (2023-01-09) to the resolution date (2023-10-24). Whether the council voted unanimously is not recorded in the PEP. Original decider wording (v0): steering council (elected five-member body), decision by council vote.

title: How annotations are evaluated: stringified versus deferred
question: How should Python evaluate annotations: make the stringified postponed form from PEP 563 the default, or replace it with lazily evaluated annotations as in PEP 649?
context: PEP 563 added a future import that stores annotations as strings, with the idea that it might become the default. Runtime users of annotations were hurt by the change. PEP 649 proposed lazy evaluation through a generated function, was blocked for years on satisfying every use case, and was accepted in 2023 for a later release; PEP 749 later fixed details.

options.label: PEP 649: evaluate annotations lazily via a generated annotate function
PEP 563: store annotations as strings, with the future import becoming the default
A lazily evaluated mapping built over stored annotation text
Keep eager evaluation at definition time (stock semantics)
Store the original source text for a source format

subQuestions: which annotation formats to support
the retirement timeline for the future import
the module that exposes annotation tooling
REPL behaviour
notableMoves: PEP 649 was blocked until a contributor proposed a technique that satisfied all runtime and typing use cases
the discussion thread was retitled to note tentative acceptance in November 2022, with formal resolution in May 2023
two polls on how to revise the PEP and a major rewrite with course corrections came before the final text
the planned release moved from 3.10 to 3.14, and PEP 563's default status never happened
PEP 749 later amended 649 and kept the future import until a stated end-of-life, then deprecation

outcome.decision: PEP 649 was resolved on 2023-05-08 and marked final for Python 3.14; PEP 563 is superseded and never became default; PEP 749 (resolved 2025-05-05) set the details and the future import's retirement path.
outcome.rationale: Stated in PEP 649: lazy evaluation fixes forward references without stringifying, keeps annotations usable at runtime, and is fast, while PEP 563 hurt runtime users and could not see local names.

chopinFit.shapeWhy: Two competing mechanisms and several rejected variants.
gaps: staged acceptance: Tentative acceptance followed by revisions and a formal acceptance months later: a staged decision with states 'tentatively accepted', 'revised after polls' and 'accepted'. The design has Open and Settled only.

superseded or moved to another thread: A chain of three records (563, then 649, then 749) where the earlier decision's planned future (becoming the default) was cancelled. There is no supersedes link between records, only Reopen on one.

blocking dependency: Blocked for years on a precondition: it could not be accepted until it satisfied every runtime and typing use case, and the unlocking technique came from another contributor. 'Blocked on a technical artefact' has no status.
formal vote: Polls were about how to revise the proposal, not about the final verdict. Meta-polls on option shape are not in the design.
staged acceptance: The decision date and the shipping release diverge by several versions. Built into shows PRs, not a planned-versus-actual release slip.
deferred: 'Just store the strings' was labelled not yet instead of rejected. An option can be deferred with a revisit hint inside a settled question, which the Also considered list cannot express.

evalUse: Multi-year supersession chain with tentative acceptance, polls on revisions, and a deferred option inside an accepted PEP.
notes: PEP 563 header, resolution and deprecation sections, PEP 649 header, rejected ideas and backward-compatibility sections, and PEP 749 abstract and background were read from clone (python/peps clone at commit 6068058). Threads for acceptance, polls and the rewrite are linked in post history but could not be fetched. The decider is not named in the PEP text, so it is left unclear even though a council decision is plausible. durationDays runs from PEP 649's creation (2021-01-11) to its resolution date (2023-05-08). The tentative-acceptance wording is inferred from a discussion thread title in the header. Original decider wording (v0): unclear (the PEP header links a resolution but does not name the decider).

Keep the eighteen-month cadence
Nine-month cadence
Keep four betas over four months and a one-month release candidate
Slow releases without freezing features at the first beta (incremental feature releases)
Designated long-term-support releases

the council's term length
the release manager's term length

title: Spelling for bounding the return type of a trait method (return type notation)
question: How should a bound name the type returned by a trait method, so async fn in traits can require Send futures: a call-like form, a path ending in return or Output, or a general type-of operator?
context: Async functions in traits need Send bounds to be expressible on the futures they return. A draft RFC proposed a call-like notation with empty parentheses; the meeting aired concerns about confusion, extensibility and a future where function arguments could be named.

options.proposedBy: nikomatsakis and the async working group

options.proposedBy: pnkfelix (as a weak preference); async WG earlier draft

A general typeof operator
Send-trait shorthand or trait transformers

outcome.decision: No decision at this meeting. The question was framed and the champion asked for anyone to defend another option strongly. The later RFC adopts m(..) after a second meeting that compared eight spellings.
outcome.rationale: Participants disliked the length of the return-path form; the Output form was liked for reusing an existing concept but seen as confusable with a future's own output; the rest marker was raised as a hedge for future argument syntax. No vote was recorded.
outcome.dissent: A participant worried about stabilising a notation that works in only one position and leaves the language irregular.
